questions.q: Why is a fixed learning rate often a poor choice for an entire training run?
options: PyTorch optimizers don't support fixed learning rates
A rate good for fast early progress is often too large later, causing the loss to oscillate instead of settling
Fixed learning rates always cause immediate NaN losses
Fixed learning rates only work with SGD, never with Adam
questions.explain: A learning rate that makes fast progress early in training is often too large later on, keeping the loss oscillating instead of letting it settle into a good minimum.

questions.q: With `StepLR(optimizer, step_size=30, gamma=0.1)`, what happens to the learning rate every 30 epochs?
options: It is multiplied by 0.1
It is increased by 30
It is reset to its original value
It is set to exactly 0.1 regardless of its previous value
questions.explain: StepLR multiplies the current learning rate by gamma every step_size epochs — here, cutting it to a tenth of its previous value every 30 epochs.

questions.q: What makes `ReduceLROnPlateau` different from `StepLR` or `CosineAnnealingLR` in how it's called?
options: It must be called before optimizer.step() instead of after
It takes no arguments at all, unlike the other two
Its .step() call requires passing a tracked metric (e.g. validation loss), rather than being called with no arguments
It can only be used with the SGD optimizer
questions.explain: ReduceLROnPlateau's step() method requires the current value of the tracked metric, e.g. scheduler.step(val_loss), whereas StepLR and CosineAnnealingLR take no arguments.

questions.q: In a typical epoch-based training loop, where should `scheduler.step()` be called for `CosineAnnealingLR`?
options: Inside the batch loop, immediately before optimizer.step()
Once per epoch, after that epoch's training loop has finished
Only once, at the very start of training
Inside the loss function definition
questions.explain: For CosineAnnealingLR (and StepLR), scheduler.step() is called once per epoch after training for that epoch completes — calling it per batch would decay the rate far faster than intended.

questions.q: Which scheduler shape decays the learning rate smoothly along a curve toward (near) zero over a fixed number of epochs, rather than in sudden jumps?
options: StepLR
ReduceLROnPlateau
CosineAnnealingLR
clip_grad_norm_
questions.explain: CosineAnnealingLR follows a cosine curve down to near zero over T_max epochs, giving a smooth decay rather than StepLR's sudden periodic drops.
